entries.clue: Detective Inspector, cop, old copper, last thing in obnoxiousness: dinosaur! (10)

indicatorNotes.last thing in: The last thing in a word is the letter it finishes on, so that single closing letter is all that is taken.

blocks.note: DI is the rank's own abbreviation on a British police warrant card
PC Plod, the policeman in the Noddy books, gives British slang its plod for an ordinary constable
o = old, the standard shortening
Cu is copper's symbol in the periodic table
the letter the word ends on

annotation.surface: A parade of policemen, senior and retired, finishing on the rudest thing anyone could say about them.
annotation.walkthrough: British slang gives 'copper' to both the policeman and the metal, and the clue wants one of each — 'cop' is the man, 'copper' the element. The colon is the seam: everything before it spells, and the word after it defines.
annotation.definitionFit: Diplodocus is one of the long-necked sauropods of the late Jurassic, so the definition names it by its kind.

entries.clue: As you heard, one who’ll stain clothes is awful (4)

indicatorNotes.As you heard: What you heard is what reached the ear, so the word is wanted for its sound rather than for the way it is spelt.

blocks.note: Somebody who colours cloth for a living is a dyer, and the trade's name is said the same way.

annotation.surface: A warning about the person whose work will leave marks all over the washing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stain' is the trap: the sentence suggests an accident with the laundry, and the clue wants the tradesman who does it deliberately. The two spellings sound identical in British speech, which is all 'as you heard' has to certify.
annotation.definitionFit: Something dire is disastrously bad — the word carries a note of calamity that awful shares.

entries.clue: Meaty spread for the Crown (4)

blocks.note: the coarse or smooth paste of liver and pork served with toast
the top of the head, the part a bald man is bald on

annotation.surface: A starter laid on for royalty.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital C dresses the second half as the monarchy, and the crown wanted is the one on top of a head. The food is pâté with two accents in French and the same four letters here, which is a licence British crosswords take freely.
annotation.definitionFit: Pâté is the meat paste spread on toast, and a pate — the same letters, no accents — is the crown of the head.

entries.clue: English actor to flourish following location of Disney World (7,5)

indicatorNotes.following: What follows a thing comes along after it, so the piece named first in the clue is the one that ends up second.

blocks.note: Walt Disney World stands at Orlando in Florida
to bloom is to flourish, of a plant or of a person

annotation.surface: An actor from England thriving since he moved to the town the theme park is in.
annotation.walkthrough: Disney World is the Florida one; Disneyland, the original, is in California, and picking the wrong coast costs the first word. In a down clue 'following' also means below, which is where the flourishing goes.
annotation.definitionFit: Orlando Bloom is the English actor of the Lord of the Rings and Pirates of the Caribbean films, so the definition names him by nationality and trade.

entries.clue: ‘Best opera? Time’s running out! Time’s running short!’ … ‘I’m not sure’ (7)

indicatorNotes.running out: What runs out of something has left it altogether, so those letters go and the rest closes up.
indicatorNotes.running short: A word run short stops before it should, so its final letter is never written.

blocks.note: OPERA minus the ERA sitting inside it
an era is a stretch of time, and that is the stretch leaving the word before it
TIME docked of its last letter
um is the noise of hesitation, printed as a word

annotation.surface: Someone pressed to name the finest opera before the clock beats them, and dithering.
annotation.walkthrough: The two cries about time are different instructions — the first takes a word for time away, the second docks a letter — and reading them as one repeated joke is what stalls the clue. Setters treat noises like 'um' as spellable words.
annotation.definitionFit: The optimum is the best available, the point at which nothing could be bettered, and 'best' is that same noun.

entries.clue: African’s somewhat smug and annoying (7)

indicatorNotes.somewhat: Somewhat is a part and not the whole, so only a part of the words that follow is taken — one unbroken run of their letters.

blocks.note: one unbroken run of letters, starting two into SMUG, swallowing AND whole and stopping two into ANNOYING

annotation.surface: A person described as rather pleased with himself and hard to put up with.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman hides words across the joins between short words, where the spaces disguise them; reading the run aloud with the gaps closed is what finds it. 'Somewhat' is doing double duty as the hedge in the description.
annotation.definitionFit: A Ugandan is a native of Uganda in East Africa, so the definition names the person by continent instead of country.

entries.clue: Nothing new about Welshman (4)

indicatorNotes.about: To turn about is to face the other way, so the word it governs is written back to front.

blocks.note: nothing is written as o, the round zero of a scoreline
NEW turned back to front

annotation.surface: A report that there is no fresh news concerning a man from Wales.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nothing new' reads as one idea and is two instructions, with 'about' looking like the preposition that would finish the phrase. Owen is the English form of the Welsh Owain, borne by Owain Glyndŵr, the last native Prince of Wales.
annotation.definitionFit: Owen is a Welsh name, first and last, so a man answering to it answers to 'Welshman'.

entries.clue: Lacks power supply in offices etc (10)

indicatorNotes.supply: Supply here is the adverb built on supple, meaning bendingly, and letters bent about do not hold the shape they were printed in.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, taken whole

annotation.surface: A power cut that has left the office with no electricity.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue turns on one word read two ways: as the noun in 'power supply' it finishes the sentence, and as the adverb from supple it is the only instruction there is. Said aloud the two are stressed on different syllables.
annotation.definitionFit: Offices are the commonest workplaces, and the 'etc' widens the definition to every other building people are employed in.

entries.clue: City’s owner, surprisingly, Banks (3,7)

indicatorNotes.surprisingly: A surprise is what you were not expecting, and these letters do not arrive in the order you were given them.

blocks.note: the five letters of OWNER redealt
an aircraft banks when it leans into its turn

annotation.surface: News that the football club's owner turns out, of all people, to be a man named Banks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'City' is the trap and the seam at once: it reads as the club the sentence gossips about, and it is the definition. 'Banks' is capitalised as a surname and wanted as the verb an aeroplane does.
annotation.definitionFit: New Orleans is the Louisiana port at the mouth of the Mississippi, home of jazz and Mardi Gras, so 'city' names it by kind.

entries.clue: Jalopy in which conductor confined? (10)

blocks.note: Sir Simon Rattle, the English conductor who led the City of Birmingham orchestra, then Berlin, then the LSO
to trap someone is to confine them

annotation.surface: A wreck of a car with a famous musician shut inside it.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: split the answer into two words and it is a named conductor shut in something. 'Conductor' pulls towards the bus and the lightning rod as well, and only the concert-hall sense is a surname.
annotation.definitionFit: A jalopy is a battered old car, and the answer is the standing word for one so worn out that it rattles its way down the road.

entries.clue: Rowers swaggered (4)

blocks.note: the eight who pull the oars, taken together as the boat's company
the old past tense of crow, and to crow over a thing is to swagger about it

annotation.surface: An eight coming down the river with something to boast about.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crew' as the past of 'crow' survives in the Bible, in 'the cock crew', and in crosswords, and almost nowhere else. A two-word clue has no link between its halves, so the split can only be in one place.
annotation.definitionFit: A boat's rowers are its crew; and to crow is to swagger and gloat, so the old past tense of that verb answers the second half.

entries.clue: Yogurt: ‘moo’ or ‘oat’, principally? Irritated parent’s testy response (2,2,4,4)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer instead of swapping for it: what is wanted is the sentence a cross parent actually says, not a noun meaning such a sentence.

indicatorNotes.principally: What comes principally comes first, so the word beside it hands over only the letter it opens with.
indicatorNotes.Irritated: Somebody irritated is stirred up and will not settle, and these letters do not settle in the order they were printed in either.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder, taken whole
the cow's noise joins the mixture exactly as written
the little joining word goes in for its own two letters
the opening letter of OAT and nothing more of it

annotation.surface: A child quizzing a parent on whether the yogurt is mostly dairy or mostly oats, and getting snapped at.
annotation.walkthrough: Oat yogurt is what lets the list read as a real question about ingredients rather than as a pile of letters. 'Principally' reaches back over the word beside it only — 'moo' and 'or' go in whole, which is the count that makes twelve.
annotation.definitionFit: Being sent to your room is the standard British parental punishment, and the phrase is what an exasperated parent snaps to end the argument.

entries.clue: Snob: one who calls everyone simply ‘Sir’ or ‘Madam’? (4-7)

annotation.definition2: one who calls everyone simply ‘Sir’ or ‘Madam’
annotation.definitionNote: The second half defines the word only when it is read literally — somebody who lets names fall — which is the opposite of what the word actually means, and the question mark is the licence for it.

blocks.note: the guest who works famous acquaintances into every conversation to look grander than he is

blocks.clueFragment: one who calls everyone simply ‘Sir’ or ‘Madam’
blocks.note: read the two words at face value and this is a man who drops names, every one of them, and falls back on the titles

annotation.surface: A man too grand ever to learn anybody's name.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drop' is the hinge: dropping a name into a conversation and dropping it from one are opposite acts, and the clue defines the word by each in turn. 'Simply' is the tell that the second half is playing it straight.
annotation.definitionFit: Parading famous acquaintances to raise yourself is one brand of snob; read literally the word is a man who lets names fall and says 'Sir' or 'Madam' instead.

entries.clue: Topless – impertinence – starting again! (10)

indicatorNotes.Topless: Something topless has lost what sat on top of it, and the top of a down answer is the letter at its head.

blocks.note: presumption is impertinence — taking a liberty nobody granted
the head letter goes, and here that letter is the P

annotation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'topless' takes the first letter, because that is the top of the answer on the page; across, the same word would have nothing to point at. The dashes are standing in for the equals sign a setter cannot print.
annotation.definitionFit: A resumption is the taking up again of something that stopped, so it names the starting again itself rather than the thing restarted.

entries.clue: Minstrel with horn going round queen, old and grumpy (10)

indicatorNotes.going round: Something going round a thing closes on both sides of it, so what it governs finishes up wrapped inside.

blocks.note: the tuba is the big brass horn at the bottom of the band
r = regina, the Latin queen printed after a British queen's name
o = old, the standard shortening
somebody dour is grim, hard and unsmiling

annotation.surface: A medieval singer circling a bad-tempered old queen.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old and grumpy' reads as one description of the queen and is two separate pieces of wordplay. Both short pieces go into the horn together, after its first letter, which is the step that hides the join.
annotation.definitionFit: A troubadour was the travelling poet-musician of medieval Provence, which is the kind of performer 'minstrel' names in general.

entries.clue: Catchy song remixed, Warmonger – No Good (7)

indicatorNotes.remixed: A remix takes the same material and puts it together another way, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: WARMONGER with the N and the G taken out, leaving seven letters to re-set
ng is the marker's shorthand for no good, and letters that are no good are the ones thrown out

annotation.surface: A remixed track credited to a band called Warmonger and written off as no good.
annotation.walkthrough: The italics are the setter printing a record sleeve — artist, then title — which is why the capitals mean nothing. Lose the two letters before shuffling anything, or you are rearranging nine to fit seven squares.
annotation.definitionFit: An earworm is the tune that lodges in the head and plays itself over, which is what a song has to be catchy to do.

entries.clue: One’s just arrived, consumed by inert gas (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a remark made about a person rather than a noun standing in for one, and the answer is the person it would be said of.

blocks.note: neon is one of the inert, or noble, gases
whatever was consumed was eaten

annotation.surface: A newcomer swallowed up by a cloud of unreactive gas.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Consumed by' does its best to look like an instruction to put one piece inside another, and the eating only sits after the gas. Neon is the crossword's inert gas of choice; argon and xenon turn up far less often.
annotation.definitionFit: A neonate is a newborn — the medical word for a baby in its first four weeks — so it is quite literally somebody who has only just turned up.

entries.clue: Sally’s beginning to wear uniform – twice, as a rule (7)

indicatorNotes.beginning to wear: Clothes go on around the wearer, so what is worn closes over the letter the name begins with rather than sitting beside it.
indicatorNotes.twice: Twice means the same thing happens again, so the uniform is put on a second time and a second letter goes in.

blocks.note: u is uniform in the NATO alphabet
the name taken whole: its first letter is the one being dressed, and the rest trails along behind
the same letter again, the uniform worn on the other side as well

annotation.surface: A girl getting into uniform for the second time today.
annotation.walkthrough: Only the first letter of the name is wrapped up; the other four come through untouched, which is why the dressing has to happen twice to make a word. Uniform is U from the NATO alphabet, the same list that gives Oscar and Romeo.
annotation.definitionFit: What happens usually is what happens as a rule — not always, but often enough to be the way to bet.

entries.clue: Flogging – initially taking seconds, becoming year – crying in pain (7)

indicatorNotes.initially taking: To take a thing initially is to take it at the front, so the letter in question is the one the word starts with.
indicatorNotes.becoming: One thing becoming another is no longer there itself — the second stands in the place the first held.

blocks.note: to flog something, in British slang, is to sell it
s = seconds, and that is the letter standing at the front
y = year, the letter that moves into the gap

annotation.surface: A whipping that starts as a matter of seconds, turns into a year of it, and is screamed through.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flogging' is the selling sense, not the whipping the surface insists on, and the sentence is built so both readings stay upright. Seconds and years are the language of a sentence handed down, which is where the picture comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: To yell is to cry out at full volume, which is what pain pulls out of somebody who cannot help it.

entries.clue: Polymeric rows, ornately twisted – essential in nutrition, primarily? (7)

annotation.definition: Polymeric rows, ornately twisted – essential in nutrition, primarily?

indicatorNotes.primarily: Primarily is at the very front, so each word of the run gives up only the letter it opens with.

blocks.clueFragment: Polymeric rows, ornately twisted – essential in nutrition
blocks.note: seven words in the order printed, each handing over its first letter

annotation.surface: A description of long molecules, elaborately coiled, that no diet can do without.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word works twice: read straight the sentence says what the answer is, and read from the front it spells it out. 'Rows' is the chemist's line of linked units, not the argument the word suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight the clue is the thing itself: a protein is a polymer, its rows of amino acids folded into elaborate shapes, and nothing lives on a diet without it.

entries.clue: Outstanding isle for exile: constantly speak up (7)

indicatorNotes.up: In a down clue up is back towards the top of the grid, so the letters are set down in the reverse of the order they were given.

blocks.note: Elba is the Mediterranean island Napoleon was exiled to in 1814
to yap is to talk on and on without stopping

annotation.surface: A splendid island to banish somebody to who never stops talking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' wants to be the compliment the island is paid, and it is the definition, meaning still unpaid. The reversal takes both pieces at once, which is why the island comes out at the back.
annotation.definitionFit: A bill that is payable has still to be paid, which is what calling a debt outstanding says of it.

entries.clue: Pages describing Scotsman Oscar having row with keyboardist (5,6)

indicatorNotes.describing: To describe a circle is to draw it round something, so the pages end up on the outside of what follows them.

blocks.note: pp is the standard short form for pages, as in a book's index
Ian is the Scottish form of John, and the crossword's usual Scot
o is Oscar in the NATO alphabet
a row of bricks laid along a wall is a layer

annotation.surface: Pages of a memoir recounting how a Scot called Oscar fell out with the man at the keys.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Row' is the layer, not the quarrel the sentence sets up — the two are spelt alike and said differently. 'Describing' is a container instruction in its geometrical sense, the one used of drawing a circle about a square.
annotation.definitionFit: The piano is a keyboard instrument, so whoever plays one is a keyboardist — the newer word for the older job.

entries.clue: Feature observed in etching (4)

indicatorNotes.observed in: What is observed in something is seen inside it, so the answer is sitting in the letters of the word that follows.

blocks.note: four letters sitting unbroken in the middle of the word, from its third to its sixth

annotation.surface: A detail of a face picked out in a print.
annotation.walkthrough: A hidden word inside a single word is harder to see than one across a gap, because no space marks where it starts. 'Feature' means a facial feature, not a feature of the picture.
annotation.definitionFit: The chin is the point of the jaw, one of the features a face is described by.

entries.clue: A woman – a flower – Everyman with chance? Almost (4)

indicatorNotes.Almost: Almost is not quite all of it, so the word arrives with its last letter missing.

blocks.note: Everyman sets this puzzle, so his name in a clue means the setter himself: I
a chance is a risk, and RISK stops one letter short

annotation.surface: A woman, a bloom and the setter's own long shot, offered one after another.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman signs the puzzle, so the word stands for I or ME wherever it turns up in it. The dashes separate three runs at the same four letters: two definitions and then the spelling of them.
annotation.definitionFit: Iris is a woman's given name and also the flag-flower of gardens and riverbanks, the one that gave its name to the eye's coloured ring.

entries.clue: The writer swindles revered figure (4)

blocks.note: the writer of the clue, speaking of himself, is I
with I as the subject the verb is con, to swindle

annotation.surface: An author cheating somebody the world looks up to.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The writer' is the setter talking about himself, the standing trick for I or ME. Once the subject is I the verb drops its s, which is how a five-letter word yields three letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An icon is an image held in reverence — the painted saint of the Orthodox church first, and by extension anybody the public venerates.

entries.clue: From prison, runs into trouble – who sees it all? (3,7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a description of the answer rather than a noun to swap for it, and the question mark is the setter's warning that it names one particular watcher.

indicatorNotes.From: Taking something from a word is taking it out of the word, so the letter named next leaves and the rest closes up.
indicatorNotes.into: Into is inwards, so what it governs goes inside the word beside it instead of alongside it.

blocks.note: the brig is a ship's prison, the navy's own lock-up
r = runs on a cricket scoreboard, and that is the letter taken out of BRIG
bother is trouble of the mild British sort

annotation.surface: An escaped convict running straight into difficulty.
annotation.walkthrough: The letter taken out of the prison is the very letter dropped into the trouble, which is the clue's economy. 'Runs' is the cricket abbreviation and also what a man leaving a cell does, so it holds both halves of the sentence together.
annotation.definitionFit: Big Brother is the all-seeing watcher of Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, whose posters promise he is watching you, so the name has come to mean whatever misses nothing.

entries.clue: Standard choice of extremes of Neoplatonism (4)

indicatorNotes.extremes of: The extremes of a word are its two ends, so its first and last letters are taken and everything between them is dropped.

blocks.note: the letter at the word's front, the first of its two extremes
a choice between two things is offered with the word or
the letter at the word's end, the other extreme

annotation.walkthrough: 'Choice' is an everyday noun doing a conjunction's work: given a choice of two, you say one or the other. Neoplatonism, the late-Roman revival of Plato's thought, is in the clue purely for the letters it starts and finishes with.
annotation.definitionFit: The norm is what is usual and expected, the level everything else gets measured against, which is standard used as a noun.

entries.clue: Meets anger flexibly for treaties (10)

indicatorNotes.flexibly: Doing a thing flexibly is bending to fit, and letters bent about do not keep the shape they were printed in.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, taken whole

annotation.surface: A negotiator running into somebody's temper and bending rather than breaking.
annotation.walkthrough: Flexibility is exactly what a negotiator is praised for, so the instruction hides inside the job description. Fodder that already means something — meeting anger — is the hardest kind to see as loose letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Treaties are the formal agreements struck between states, so the definition names the answer by its weightiest kind.
